summary: The Acoustic impedance calculator turns the speed of sound, the specific acoustic impedance (z) and the intensity reflection coef. (R) into density (ρ). It suits a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Acoustic impedance calculator work?
sections.html:
The Acoustic impedance calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports density (ρ) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the find, choose material and the material 1); then you type in the speed of sound (c), the specific acoustic impedance (z) (2), the intensity reflection coef. (R) (2) and the intensity reflection coef. (R) (4).

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Acoustic impedance calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Density (ρ)=1000000 × specific acoustic impedance (z) ÷ speed of sound (c)
Intensity reflection coef. (R)=(specific acoustic impedance 1 (z₁) − specific acoustic impedance 2 (z₂) ^ 2) ÷ (specific acoustic impedance 1 (z₁) + specific acoustic impedance 2 (z₂) ^ 2)
Specific acoustic impedance 1 (z₁)=specific acoustic impedance 2 (z₂) × (2 × the square root of (intensity reflection coef. (R)) − intensity reflection coef. (R) − 1) ÷ (intensity reflection coef. (R) − 1)
Intensity transmission coef. (T)=4 × specific acoustic impedance 1 (z₁) × specific acoustic impedance 2 (z₂) ÷ (specific acoustic impedance 1 (z₁) + specific acoustic impedance 2 (z₂) ^ 2)
Specific acoustic impedance 1 (z₁)=specific acoustic impedance 2 (z₂) × (-intensity transmission coef. (T) + 2 × the square root of (1 − intensity transmission coef. (T)) + 2) ÷ intensity transmission coef. (T)
Specific acoustic impedance 2 (z₂)=specific acoustic impedance 1 (z₁) × (-intensity transmission coef. (T) + 2 × the square root of (1 − intensity transmission coef. (T)) + 2) ÷ intensity transmission coef. (T)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Acoustic impedance, opening in megarayls

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Acoustic impedance calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the speed of sound, the specific acoustic impedance (z) and the intensity reflection coef. (R) — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Acoustic impedance calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns density (ρ), derived from the speed of sound, the specific acoustic impedance (z) and the intensity reflection coef. (R). Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Acoustic impedance calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the speed of sound, the specific acoustic impedance (z) and the intensity reflection coef. (R), which is 9 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter specific acoustic impedance (z) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Specific acoustic impedance (z) opens in megarayls and the chip beside it offers 4 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (4 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Specific acoustic impedance (z) = 0 MRayl. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Acoustic impedance calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
